lines: Notice that nothing here actually malfunctioned.
The first request worked. The acknowledgement that should have confirmed that simply never made it back. Everything after that point is a reasonable response to incomplete information.
The customer paid for a system behaving correctly, twice.
Before choosing, separate what the pipeline's own guarantee could possibly reach from what it can't.
Whatever happens inside the pipeline's walls is one question. What happens the moment a request leaves to talk to someone else's system is a completely different one.
answer: The fix is a value sent with the retry, not a stronger broker.
An idempotency key lets the processor recognize the second attempt as the same request, not a new charge.
No internal guarantee, however strong, can reach past the pipeline's own boundary to fix this on its own.

lines: Watch what this argument actually rules out, because it's narrower than it sounds.
It doesn't say a lower layer's reliability feature is useless. It says that feature alone can never be the whole answer, because only the application actually knows what correctness means here.
A reliable-sounding broker is, at best, a head start, not a finish line.
Pay attention to what's actually being chosen here, not just named.
Retry, and you might deliver twice. Don't retry, and you might lose the message outright. Every system on a lossy link is choosing one of exactly these two risks.
There's no quiet third option hiding anywhere in here.
Notice that the two runs differ in exactly one thing.
Same timeout, same retry, same lost acknowledgement. The only thing that changes is whether the processor has a key to check the second attempt against.
That single difference is the entire gap between a double charge and a safe no-op.
Carry forward what actually changed here, because it isn't the delivery.
The message still arrives twice, exactly as before. What's different is that twice now costs the same as once.
That's the whole trick behind the phrase. It was never about making delivery stronger.
Think about what each of these two systems is actually protecting against.
Kafka ties a producer's output to the consumer's offset so neither can exist without the other. Flink ties an external write to its own checkpoint the same way.
Different products, same refusal to let one half of a pair survive without the other.
Separate what just got fixed from what never could be.

Everything inside this topic's three mechanisms now has an atomic answer. The moment a side effect crosses out to a system this pipeline doesn't control, none of those three mechanisms are even in the room anymore.
Carry forward the shape of the whole answer, not three separate fixes.
Delivery alone was never going to be exactly-once. It took an idempotent write to make a duplicate harmless, and an atomic commit to close the one crash window left inside the pipeline.
Outside that boundary, none of it reaches.
Before answering, ask what an idempotency key is actually checked against, and by whom.
It only does anything where something on the other end is actually looking at it and comparing.
answer: The key protects exactly the write that checks for it. A confirmation email the retry also triggers, with nothing on the email side watching for repeats, goes out again regardless.
The key fixed one effect. It never touched the other one.
